question: Who is Coach Mike, and why should I listen to him?
answer:
Michael LoCicero. Six decades developing goaltenders.

He was watching goaltending before he could sit up on his own — propped upright with pillows behind him and either side of him, in front of a black-and-white television, Hockey Night in Canada. He wasn't two years old.

There were no goalie coaches then. No clinics, no positional systems written down for anyone to follow. "Before there were goalie coaches, there were goalies — trying to figure it out alone. I was one of them."

So he worked it out himself, and how he did it is why the system exists. He wasn't copying the professionals — he was asking why it worked. "I needed to dissect the Why For's, to master the How To's, and to discern the When For's of every technique and decision. Copying was never an option."

He created the Seven Marker Program in 1977, at twenty-two, while still playing. He retired from playing in 1986 and wrote the original manual that decade.

He describes what he found as a thousand-piece puzzle with no picture on the box. "So I created a border. Then filled in the pieces — one Skill Category at a time."

That's the reason to listen. Not the years — the fact that a man who had to build it from nothing knows why every piece sits where it does.

question: How do I know if I'm on my angle?
answer:
Before the answer, the thing underneath it: you have to build a relationship to the ice you play on. The net. The crease. The white ice beyond it, where the markers live. A goalie who doesn't own those relationships is guessing, and no definition fixes that.

Inside that relationship, a good angle is your position relative to the puck and the net, so that the net available to the shooter is as small as it can be.

But here is the part most goalies never hear. A good angle is not static. It moves with the puck and with the players. You are not finding a spot and holding it - you are staying in a relationship that keeps changing.

And you check it without looking. That's the Feel Factor. Most goalies glance at the post, reach for it, and in that half-second the play has moved on. When your markers are trained, you stop checking and start knowing.

Feeling is the goal. The glance is the enemy.

question: My coach says I was "out of position." What does the right position actually look like?
answer:
It's a fair thing for a coach to say and it's rarely a useful thing to hear, because it tells you that something was wrong without telling you what.

Right position has two parts and three pieces. The front of your body centred to the puck. Your back centred to the net. That is a Good Angle, and it is geometry, not feel.

Get both and you create coverage. The shooter is choosing from what you have left him, which is very little.

Get one and not the other and you look square while being beaten. Skating backwards especially, a goalie drifts off the line connecting the puck to the net and opens a side without knowing it.

So next time, ask your coach which piece was missing. And in the meantime - this is exactly what the markers are for. They turn "out of position" into a specific, fixable place on the ice.

question: Why is goalie skating different from player skating?
answer:
Because a player skates to get somewhere. A goalie skates to arrive in a position to make a save, still balanced, still able to move again.

A player can be off balance at the end of a stride and it costs him nothing. A goalie who arrives off balance has already lost the save.

So we teach different things. Edge control. Weight distribution. The T-push, pivots, direct movement along real travel lanes rather than wandering. Toe and heel work. Push-pull - extend then retract, no stagnant push, no over-extension you can't recover from.

And stopping matters more than starting. Anyone can go. Arriving under control is the skill.

That is why team skating time only partly serves you. It is good work and it is not your work. Goalie skating is not player skating.

question: Why am I gassed by the third period?
answer:
Usually because you are spending movement you did not need to spend.

That's what Movement, Energy and Time means. No wasted movement, no wasted energy, no wasted time - and they are linked. Waste one and you waste all three. A goalie who moves twice to get where one move would have taken him has paid twice, and by the third period the bill arrives.

So the question isn't your fitness first. It's your efficiency. Are you set before the release, or scrambling after it? Are you taking the direct line, or drifting and correcting?

Fitness matters too, and we chart it - stretching, conditioning, aerobic and anaerobic work, sleep, nutrition. But a fit goalie who moves badly still runs out.

Maximum coverage, minimal movement. That's not a style. It's an energy policy.

question: My goalie is always half a second late. Is that slow reflexes, or something we can fix?
answer:
Almost always it's fixable, and almost always it isn't reflexes.

Late usually means the read started late. The eyes arrived after the puck did. That's not speed - that's sequence, and sequence can be trained.

We teach it in order: Visual, then Mental, then Physical. You see it, you read it, you respond. Sequential, never simultaneous. A goalie who tries to move while still working out what's happening is the goalie who looks half a second slow.

The other common cause is position. If he's in the wrong place, he has further to travel and no amount of quickness closes that gap. Half a second late is often just two feet out.

Test it honestly before you conclude anything: is he set before the release? Most "slow" goalies are not.

question: What do I do when the puck goes behind my net?
answer:
You understand how to play both the man and the puck. That understanding is the whole skill.

Most goalies have never been taught it as one thing. They track the puck and have no idea what he is setting up. Or they watch him and get beaten by a puck that went somewhere they were not expecting. Both of those are a goalie reacting to one half of a situation.

And the two are not always in the same place. The puck can be in one spot and his body somewhere else entirely - that is not an accident, that is him working on you.

Understanding both means you know what each of them can do, and what the two of them together make possible from where they are. Once you know that, you are not tracking anything. You already know the short list of what can happen next.

Where he is and where the puck is tell you that. It is what the zones are for.

And once you accept that it is your house, the whole thing gets simpler. He is a visitor. He does not get to decide how it goes in there.

question: How do I stop one bad goal from wrecking the rest of my game?
answer:
By having somewhere to put it.

The goalie who spirals is the goalie carrying it with nowhere to set it down. So you build a place: reflect after, not during. During the game there is only the next read.

Understand what actually happened, and be honest - some goals are your positioning, some are your read, and some were going in against anybody. Deciding which is which is a skill, and it's the difference between learning and punishing yourself.

You will have that answer properly after, when you look. The video never lies, and it is usually kinder than your memory.

And know this: failure is not part of this system. A goal against is information. Nothing is being subtracted from you.

question: I've had lessons before and nothing stuck. Why would this be different?
answer:
Because most training goes stale and nobody tells you that's what happened.

You learn something in October. You don't touch it. By January it's gone, so you learn it again - and that is why so many goalies feel like they're running on the spot after years of lessons.

This system reaffirms what you've acquired rather than letting it drift. That is the key, and it is the actual difference.

The second difference is that it's a record, not a session. A lesson ends. This doesn't - what you understood last season is still here next season, and the season after.

The third is that it's a system rather than a style. A goalie taught a style has to rebuild it when his body changes. A goalie taught a system carries it across.

question: How is this different from a goalie camp?
answer:
A camp is a week. This is a record.

Camps are good - we run on-ice work ourselves, and concentrated in-person time accelerates things nothing else can. But a camp ends, and what you learned there lives in your memory, which lies in the same direction every time.

Here, the work is kept. Your charts, your answers, your adjustments, your lows and your highs. Season three is worth more because season one exists.

That's the whole difference. A camp gives you a week of coaching. This gives you a history that keeps serving you - and it doesn't forget you between visits.

question: Does this work if I'm not on a competitive team?
answer:
Yes, and at house league level some of it matters more, not less.

The systems don't change with the level. Where you stand, how you move, how you read - those are the same problems whether the shooter is thirteen or twenty. Level decides the pace. It doesn't decide whether it applies.

You don't need a team at all, in fact. As long as you can get ice and a shooter or two, we can guide the work. Plenty of goalies do their most important development away from a roster.

And understanding where to stand is worth more at house league than anywhere else, because almost nobody there has been taught it.

question: What are the 8 Pillars?
answer:
Eight angles on one goalie.

1. MindSet - control what is inside, or you will not control what is outside.
2. Skating Tech - goalie skating, which is not player skating.
3. The 7 Angle-Marker System - positional certainty above the icing line.
4. The 6 Zone - 7 Point System(TM) - net management below the icing line.
5. Form Tech - how you set, how you seal, what your body actually does.
6. The Game Performance Charting System - your record, in your own words.
7. The Practice System - how you use the ice you get, including the dead time.
8. Lifestyle & Hockey - the athlete underneath the goalie.

They are not eight subjects to get through. They lean on each other. Your skating decides your angles. Your angles decide what your form has to survive. Your mind decides whether any of it holds up in the third period.

You do not have to start at one. You have to start somewhere honest.

question: What is the Development Loop?
answer:
Chart, directive, practice, chart.

You chart what actually happened. The chart shows where the gap is. That gap becomes one directive - one thing to work on, not five. You practise that directive. Then you chart again and see whether it moved.

That's the loop, and it's the engine of the whole system. It's why the charting isn't paperwork - it's the thing that tells you what to do next.

Most goalies practise whatever the session happens to contain. A goalie in this loop practises what his own evidence says he needs.

question: What is Opportunity Time?
answer:
The minutes in a team practice when the puck is nowhere near you - and you train anyway.

Here's where it came from. As a player I asked my coaches for permission to use the time that was, for me, wasted. When the team went to the boards for a drill explanation, I'd go to my net and work. When the team had a twenty-minute skating block, I'd skate part of it and then go work my own game - because goalie skating is not player skating.

That's the mechanic, and the first part matters: you ask your coach in advance. This is a cooperative arrangement, not going freelance.

Then you work your designated activity - the directive you came in with. Not watching. Not thinking about it. Physically at your net, training.

A bored goalie is a goalie who hasn't been given a job. Give yourself one before you step on the ice.

question: What does "Built Not Born" mean?
answer:
It means nobody arrives with this. It gets built.

There is a belief in hockey that goalies are born - that the good ones have something you either have or you don't. I have spent six decades watching that be wrong.

What actually separates goalies is understanding, applied consistently, over time. That can be taught, and it can be built, and I have watched it built in goalies who were told they didn't have it.

Greatness is built, not born. That is the philosophy the whole system sits on.

question: What is the 5-Star Engine?
answer:
The ladder a goalie climbs, and the destination is not what people expect.

One star, Learning. You're taking it in.
Two, Self-Evaluation. You can look at your own game honestly.
Three, Self-Awareness. You know what you're doing while you're doing it.
Four, Self-Adjusting. You fix it in the moment, without being told.
Five, Self-Coaching.

Self-Coaching does not mean you no longer need a coach. It means you know what support you need and you can ask for it precisely. That's a higher skill than obedience, and it's the one that lasts after I'm gone from your development.

question: What is the Mind-Vault?
answer:
Where the valuable things are kept.

It has three jobs. It stores and retrieves - the reads, the corrections, the things you've already solved, so you don't solve them twice. It filters the noise, because a goalie hears a great deal in a season and most of it isn't useful. And it masters the reset, which is how you get from one moment to the next without carrying the last one.

It's the discipline of building a place where only the most valuable foundational thoughts and behaviours are kept. For game performance, and for life in general.

If you cannot control what's inside, you cannot control what's outside.

question: What is charting, and why does it matter so much here?
answer:
Charting is you, recording what actually happened, in your own words and your own ratings.

It matters because memory lies. Every goalie remembers the game he thinks he played, and the chart remembers the game he played. The gap between those two is the Technical Eye, and closing it is most of the development.

The chart is a mirror, not a test. Nobody is grading you and there is nothing to fail. If you're not honest in it, the only person you fool is yourself, and you're the one it's for.

Then it accumulates. Period by period, game by game, season by season. And a rating that dips doesn't get you told off - it opens the lessons that lift it.

question: What does "Movement, Energy and Time" mean?
answer:
No wasted movement. No wasted energy. No wasted time.

And they're not three separate rules - they're one. Waste one and you waste all three. An unnecessary movement costs energy, and the energy costs you time you needed later.

It's the efficiency engine of everything we teach. When you see a goalie who looks calm and always seems to be there already, you are not watching quick feet. You are watching someone who stopped spending movement he didn't need.

question: What does "Visual, Mental and Physical" mean?
answer:
The order in which a save actually happens.

You see it. You read it. You respond.

Sequential, never simultaneous - and the order is the teaching. A goalie who moves before he's read is guessing. A goalie who reads without having properly seen is guessing earlier.

Most goalies who look slow are not slow. They started at Physical.

question: What is the Feel Factor?
answer:
Knowing exactly where you are in your net without looking for it.

Most goalies check. They glance at the post, they reach for it - and in that half-second the play has moved. When your markers are trained, you stop checking and you start knowing.

That is the Feel Factor, and it is built, not born.

Feeling is the goal. The glance is the enemy.

question: What is a Good Angle?
answer:
Two parts, three pieces, and it's geometry rather than feel.

Part one: the front of your body centred to the puck.
Part two: your back centred to the net - goal line centred to post.

Get both and you have created coverage. The shooter sees very little net and has to be near perfect to use it.

It is not static. It moves as the puck moves and as the players move, so you are holding a relationship, not standing on a spot.

And it does a second job people forget: a good angle keeps your sightlines clear, so you can see through traffic instead of being blinded by it.

question: What is an Intelligent Athletic Goaltender?
answer:
The goalie this system is built to produce.

Athletic, because the position demands it - agility, flexibility, strong legs, endurance, hand-eye and leg-eye coordination, the ability to track and to recover.

Intelligent, because athleticism without understanding runs out. This is a goalie who knows why he is where he is, who reads rather than reacts, who can look at his own game honestly and adjust it.

Put simply: he decides. Everyone else reacts. An Intelligent Athletic Goaltender knows the options, anticipates the play, and dictates the terms.

question: What is Designated Training?
answer:
Targeted work drawn from what your charts say needs attention.

Not a general session. Not whatever the practice happens to contain. One specific thing, chosen because your own evidence pointed at it.

That's what makes it different from ordinary practice. Ordinary practice is exposure. Designated Training is treatment.

And it's what you take into Opportunity Time - you arrive at the rink already knowing what your job is today.

question: What is Mental Math, and what has it got to do with goaltending?
answer:
It's your brain computing a moving object without you consciously doing any of it.

Where it's going. How fast. Where it will be when you get there. You are not calculating that on purpose - and yet you get it right constantly, in every part of your life.

I learned this away from the rink. My father and my uncles were pitchers in high-level baseball, so catching was in our house early - and catching, and fielding a ball, is fantastic training for it. The reads and the reaction are the same computation the position needs. Different object.

That's the Mental step in Visual, Mental, Physical. And the Feel Factor is that same math run so many times it no longer needs looking.

Which is why we ask what other sports you've played. You may already own more of this machinery than you know.

question: My kid wants to be a goalie. Is that a good idea?
answer:
If it's their idea, yes. If it's yours, be careful.

This is the position with the most responsibility on the ice and the most exposure. It asks for commitment, dedication, perseverance, and the ability to survive the lows. A goalie who chose it will find those things. A goalie who was put there rarely does.

What it gives back is unusual. Quick reflexes and coordination, yes - but mostly it builds character under pressure in a way almost nothing else at that age does. Goalies learn accountability early because there is nowhere to hide.

They also become leaders. How the goalie goes, the bench follows.

So the honest answer: it's a wonderful thing to be, and it is not an easy thing to be. If it's their idea, back them.
