question: What age should my child start - and is there an age that's too late?
answer:
There's no bad age to start understanding the position, and there is no age that's too late.

Young goalies can begin with the ideas well before they can execute them. Knowing where you are, why you're there, what you're looking at - a child can learn that, and it costs nothing physically.

And older is not too late. A goalie who arrives at fifteen with no system has more to gain from one, not less, because everything he's been doing has been guesswork and he can feel it.

What actually matters is not the age. It's whether they want it.

question: My kid is crushed after a bad game. What do I say in the car?
answer:
Less than you think.

The car ride home is the most important twenty minutes of the week and most parents fill it with coaching. Your goalie already knows what went wrong - they lived it, and they've been replaying it since the second period.

Ask one question: "What did you see out there?" Then listen.

You are not their goalie coach. You are the person who makes the rink feel safe to come back to.

And if they ask you not to talk about it - respect that. That's not shutting you out. That's a young athlete managing themselves, which is exactly what we're trying to build.

question: My kid's coach has never played the position. Now what?
answer:
That describes most coaches, and it isn't a criticism of them.

Almost everyone coaching minor hockey played out. Nobody trained them for the one position that doesn't do what the others do. They're volunteers doing their best with a position nobody taught them.

What changes things is shared language. When your goalie can say what he's working on this week, his coach can support it without knowing the position. That's most of the gap closed, and it costs the coach nothing.

We are the team behind the team. We're not replacing anybody.

question: How do I know if my child is actually improving, when the scoreboard says otherwise?
answer:
Because the scoreboard is the worst measure of a goalie you could pick.

A goalie can be excellent in a loss and lucky in a win. Judge either one by the result and you'll be wrong about half the time, and your child will know you're wrong.

What you can actually watch: is he in position more often? Is he calmer after a goal against? Is he talking to his defence? Does he look like he knows what he's doing rather than hoping?

And then there's the record. That's the point of the charting - you're not relying on impressions. You can see what he understood in October and owns by February.

Measure them by their progress, not the scoreboard.

question: Should my kid play other sports too?
answer:
Yes. And it does more for the position than most people realise.

Anything where you catch, field, block or intercept something moving fast is training the same computation goaltending needs. Baseball especially - my father and my uncles were pitchers, and catching was in our house early. The reads and the reactions in fielding a ball are fantastic for what I call Mental Math.

Different object, same brain doing the work.

Beyond that, other sports build the athlete underneath the goalie - agility, coordination, balance, endurance. And they give a young athlete somewhere else to be, which protects them from the burnout that takes so many of them at fifteen.

You are building an athlete first. The goalie is what the athlete does.

question: How much does the equipment matter?
answer:
More than almost anything, and not for the reason people think.

Protection first, and protection is the whole point of it. Getting hit by a puck is not fun and it hurts.

Here is what most families never connect: poor equipment raises the fear factor. A goalie who does not trust his gear flinches. He turns his head. He gets small when he should get big. Fear of getting hurt is not a foundation for development — it's the opposite of one, and no amount of coaching gets past it.

Buy the protection. Everything else is negotiable.

On cost, two things worth knowing. The better the first purchase, the better the trade-in or the resale — so you are realistically paying market rate once, not repeatedly, until the goalie graduates to adult equipment. And even then there is resale.

And on being a new goalie parent, plainly: there is a stigma that arrives with the position when the skill level isn't sharp yet. Hero, or the label of "not a good goalie" — and the label sticks. Understand that it belongs to the development period and not to your child. Every goalie who is good now went through it.

We are building a place in our community pages where families can post used equipment to sell or to buy. We take nothing from it. It's a noticeboard, not a store — you post, you arrange it between yourselves. It costs us nothing and it saves families real money.

question: My child is the backup this season. Is the year wasted?
answer:
Not unless you let it be.

Being number two is one of the challenges this position asks you to accept, and it's on our list precisely because it's so common and so badly handled.

The wasted version is the goalie who sits and waits. The valuable version works - in practice, with a directive, with someone charting. He watches his partner deliberately, taking what's useful. He stays ready, because the call comes without warning and he wants to be the one who was prepared for it.

And there's something you can only learn here: handling it well. Coaches notice the backup who works and supports his partner. That reputation follows a goalie for years.

Encourage him to talk to his coach honestly about what he needs to do. Then keep working.

question: What will I actually be able to see?
answer:
Their record, as it builds.

What they're working on right now. What they've charted after games and practices. Where they rate themselves and how that's moved. What they've locked in and what's still developing. And time on the site, so you know whether the work is actually happening.

You'll get updates as it happens rather than having to ask.

What you won't see by default is what your goalie writes privately about himself - and that's deliberate. Some of what a young athlete puts in here is honest in a way they wouldn't be out loud, and that honesty is what makes the whole thing work. Protecting it protects the value.

How you use what you can see is between you and your goalie.

question: How do I support my goalie without coaching him?
answer:
Support the person. Leave the position to us.

You don't need to know the technical side, and trying to supply it usually backfires - because if what you say contradicts what he's being taught, you've put him in the middle.

What only you can do: be steady. Be the same after a loss as after a win. Make sure he's fed, rested and got his gear. Ask what he saw rather than telling him what you saw. Get him to the rink and let the rink be his.

And measure him by his progress rather than the score.

That's not a smaller job than coaching. It's the bigger one.

question: Am I pushing too hard?
answer:
The fact that you're asking says a great deal, and most parents never do.

Here's the test I'd use. Is the pressure coming from him, or from you? A goalie who is driving this will get himself to the rink. A goalie who is being driven needs you to get him there - and if you're the engine, you'll feel it as constant effort.

Some signs worth being honest about: he doesn't want to talk about games. He seems relieved when practice is cancelled. He performs worse when you're watching than when you're not.

None of that makes you a bad parent. It usually means someone who cares a great deal has pushed a bit past where the caring lands well.

What we ask of parents is simple: support them and stay off the ice. Avoid the temptation to coach from the stands. And measure them by their progress, not the scoreboard.

The goalies who last are the ones who chose it. Your job is to keep it theirs.

question: What does this really ask of me - time, driving, money, all of it?
answer:
Straight answer, because you deserve one before you commit.

Time: fifteen minutes a day from your goalie is a real amount and it makes a difference. Not from you. This is his work, done on his own.

From you: the same driving you're already doing, and twenty minutes of listening on the way home.

Money: the registration is one payment, and the subscription can be switched off in the off-season so you're not paying for months nobody uses. Equipment is the real cost of this position and always has been - and buying protection properly the first time costs less over a career than replacing cheap gear.

The thing this asks that people don't expect is patience. Development is not linear and there will be a stretch where nothing seems to be moving. The record will show you it is.

question: Why do I go down too early?
answer:
Because going down feels like doing something, and standing still feels like doing nothing. It isn't.

Ask yourself one honest question, and you probably can't answer it yet: are you going down before the shot? Most goalies who drop early genuinely cannot tell you. That's not a character flaw - nobody has ever shown them.

Here's the cost. Down early means the shooter is choosing from what's left, and what's left is up. You've made his decision easy.

The fix isn't "stay up." It's earlier than that. It's whether you're set before the release, and whether your set-crouch is the right one for where the puck actually is. A higher set-crouch when the puck is further out. A lower one when it's close, or when you need to seal.

Maximum coverage, minimal movement. If you're down before he's shot, you've spent the movement and bought no coverage.

question: Why do I keep getting beat short side?
answer:
Almost always because you are not where you think you are.

Skating backwards, a goalie can drift off the line connecting the puck to the net and unknowingly open one side. It feels square the whole way. It isn't.

That's the whole answer, and it's why the markers exist. A goalie who knows where he is doesn't need to guess whether he's square - he knows, without looking, because he's built the relationship to his net, his crease and the white ice around it.

Short side isn't a hole in your game. It's a hole in your information.

question: How do I stop guessing?
answer:
First, know which one you're doing, because they're two different problems.

Over-anticipating is deciding too early. You predict the play and commit before it happens, and a clever player will take that from you every time.

Over-reacting is responding too fast to something that already happened. Unnecessary movement, and now you're out of position with the net open behind you.

One is prediction. The other is reaction. Both leave you somewhere you didn't choose to be.

The answer to both is reading rather than guessing - the stick, the eyes, the hands, the body. Is he in shooting position, or is he stick handling? That's a read, and reads can be trained. Guessing can't.

question: How do I tell if he's going to shoot or pass?
answer:
You read his body and you read his options, and you keep them separate.

Is he in shooting position? Then he can shoot at any moment. There's no wind-up you're waiting for. Respect that and stay honest.

Is he stick handling? Different animal. From there he can deke, or he has to transfer into release mode - forehand or backhand. That transfer is a moment, and moments are what you read.

But be careful with the assumption. Some players are very clear shooters and will take it the second you give them anything.

And this matters more than people think: the man and the puck are not always parallel. The puck can be in one place and his body somewhere else entirely. You are reading both, not one.

question: How do I control my rebounds?
answer:
We break it into three phases, and most goalies only ever think about the middle one.

Phase one is anticipation and positioning. Before the shot. Where you are, how you're set, what you know about this shooter. A poor base gives you an uncontrolled rebound before the puck has even arrived.

Phase two is direction and absorption. Either you kill it, or you send it somewhere it can't hurt you - the corners, behind the net. Soft hands, stick placement, body position. You are deciding where that puck goes, not hoping.

Phase three is recovery. If there is a rebound, you're back to a ready position for the second shot - quick push, angle adjusted, eyes still on the puck.

And a strategic piece most goalies miss: sometimes the right answer is to freeze it. Kill the momentum, get the line change. That's a decision, not a failure.

Where the rebound goes was decided before the shot. That's the part nobody tells you.

question: How do I stop pucks I can't see?
answer:
You don't stop what you can't see. You get to where you can see it.

That's what a good angle is actually for, and almost nobody explains it this way. Angle isn't only about covering net - it's about sightlines. Positioned properly, you can see through and around traffic and track the puck. Positioned badly, you've blindfolded yourself.

Our Screen System teaches three things: read the screen - how many bodies, where they are, what they're taking from you. Adjust - look through, around or over, and move to buy the sightline. And anticipate the deflection, because a screened puck changes direction more often than a clean one.

A higher set-crouch helps here. It's the one that maximises vision over a screen.

question: How do I play a breakaway?
answer:
A breakaway is not one skill. It's every skill you have, arriving at once.

The mental game, the physical game, and the relationship between you, the puck and the man — all of it, compressed into about two seconds.

The core of it is gap closing. As the player breaks in, you challenge — you come out to take the net away from him. Do it well and one of two things happens, and both of them are wins for you. Either you force him into an incredible shot — the kind that has to be perfect to beat you — or you force him to run out of real estate, and then he has to shoot or deke with no room left to do either properly.

Now the read, and this is where breakaways are won.

Is he in shooting position, or is he stick handling?

In shooting position, he can shoot at any moment. There is no wind-up you're waiting for. Respect that and stay honest.

Stick handling is a different animal. From there he can deke — or he has to transfer into release mode, forehand or backhand. That transfer is a moment, and moments are what you read.

But be careful with the assumption, because some players are very clear shooters and will take it the second you give them anything.

And here is the whole game inside the game: if he gets you to bite, the advantage is his. You've committed, he hasn't. From there you need a counter move — or a desperation attempt is in the cards, and desperation is what you were trying to avoid by reading properly in the first place.

So: close the gap, take his room, and don't buy what he's selling until he's paid for it.

One more thing. Skating backwards, a goalie can drift off the line connecting the puck to the net and unknowingly open one side. It feels square the whole way. It isn't. On a breakaway, that is usually the goal.

question: Why do I get scored on right after a big save?
answer:
Because you're still in the save you just made.

The big one is emotional. It lifts you, it lifts your bench, and for about two seconds you're admiring it instead of playing. Meanwhile the puck is loose and nobody else stopped.

This is the same skill as moving on from a goal against, just faster. Reflect after, not during. The save is over the instant it's over.

It's also a rebound problem more often than anyone admits. Phase three exists for exactly this moment - recover, re-set, find the puck. A great save with no recovery is half a save.

question: What do I do on a two-on-one?
answer:
You play the puck carrier and you trust your defenceman to take the pass. That's the arrangement, and it only works if it's actually been agreed.

So talk. Direct your defence, call the threat, tell them what you want. That's part of the position, not an extra.

Then read: is he in shooting position, or is he carrying? If he's shooting, you're honest with the shooter. If he's looking to pass, you stay on your line and you do not lunge across before the puck does.

The mistake is trying to cover both. Cover both and you cover neither.

question: How do I stop over-committing when he dekes me?
answer:
Understand what he's actually doing. He's selling, and over-committing is buying.

If he gets you to bite, the advantage is his. You've committed, he hasn't. From there you need a counter move, or a desperation attempt is in the cards - and desperation is what proper reading was supposed to prevent.

So close the gap and take his room. When you challenge, you force him into an incredible shot or you run him out of real estate. Both are wins for you.

And don't buy what he's selling until he's paid for it.

question: How do I play through traffic in front of me?
answer:
Three jobs, in this order.

Read the screen. How many bodies, where they are, what they're taking from your sightline. That's information, and you can gather it before the shot comes.

Adjust to see. Through, around or over. Small movements to buy the sightline, because a puck you can see is a puck you can play.

Anticipate the deflection. Screened pucks change direction. Expect it rather than being surprised by it.

The set-crouch matters here. Higher for vision over the screen. Lower and wider when you're sealing the ice in heavy traffic. Two different crouches for two different problems, and knowing which is which is the skill.

One more thing worth knowing: some players screen you honestly and some make a career of disrupting you. Know which ones you're dealing with and keep your composure either way.

question: Why do I get beaten on the first shot of the game?
answer:
Because your body arrived and your read didn't.

Your warm-up got you loose. It did not necessarily get your eyes working, and the eyes are what make the first save.

That's what a pre-game routine is for, and it's more than stretching. Warm-up drills that sharpen the reflexes, mental preparation, visualisation of the situations you're about to face. You are rehearsing the read, not just the movement.

Be honest about it too - the first shot often comes when you are still deciding how the game feels. Decide before the puck drops.

question: What do I need to get started?
answer:
Less than you think, and there are no restrictions on the automated side. If you want in, you're in.

Registration is a questionnaire, and it matters. Name, age, level, and why you're here — plus one screen that tells us whether the goalie is driving this or being driven. That's not paperwork. It's where your first directive comes from. Nobody is handed a generic plan.

A phone is enough to begin — and almost nobody doesn't have one.

Video is optional and it's an upgrade. Video analysis is added to your program as a purchase, not bundled in. A parent shoots it, or somebody you choose, under our instruction — we map out exactly what to film and how, and you'll see examples from Coach Mike's own footage so you're not guessing.

And you don't need a team. As long as you can get ice and a shooter or two, we can guide the work with our instructional content. Plenty of goalies do their most important development away from a roster.

question: Is this online only, or is there on-ice coaching too?
answer:
Both — and I'll be straight with you about the scale of it.

Right now I am the sole provider. There is no staff. That will change, but I won't promise you something I can't personally stand behind today.

What exists now is come to us, or we come to you. The stronger of the two is coming to us: a three-day, five-day or longer accelerated learning experience — concentrated, in person, with the systems taught properly rather than in forty-minute pieces.

The platform is where the understanding is built and where your record lives. The on-ice is where it gets accelerated. They aren't alternatives.

question: Do I need ice time to use this?
answer:
No, and that surprises people.

A large part of this is understanding, and understanding is built off the ice. The knowledge, the reads, the charting, the review of your own games - none of that needs a rink.

When you do get ice, you use it better, because you arrive with a directive instead of hoping the session contains something useful.

And you don't need much. A shooter or two and some ice is enough for real work. Plenty of goalies do their most important development away from a roster.

The ice makes it faster. It doesn't make it possible.

question: What level is this for - house league or competitive?
answer:
Both, and the systems don't change between them.

Where you stand, how you move, how you read the play - those are the same problems at every level. Level decides the pace. It doesn't decide whether it applies.

At competitive level the margins are thinner, so positional certainty matters more. At house league, simply understanding where to stand is worth an enormous amount, because almost nobody there has been taught it.

I have never met a goalie who was too good for the fundamentals or too raw for them.

question: Will Coach Mike see my work himself?
answer:
I'm going to answer this honestly rather than the way it would sell best.

I don't promise personal review, because I won't promise something I can't guarantee to everyone. If there are a thousand goalies on this platform, I cannot look at a thousand records the way they deserve, and I would rather tell you that now than apologise later.

What I do is reach out. A call, a message, a chat — unannounced, because I'd rather surprise you than schedule you. It happens, and it will keep happening.

And every question the system cannot answer comes to me personally. You ask, you leave your address, and inside twenty-four hours you get my answer — and that answer then becomes part of the library for every goalie who comes after you.

As this grows, so does what I can offer. When the company can support it, personal review becomes a real, defined option rather than a promise I can't keep.

question: How long before I see a difference?
answer:
There's no firm number, and anyone who gives you one is selling.

You get out of this what you put into it. Apply it, be consistent, and progress begins on day one — it doesn't wait for a milestone.

A month at fifteen minutes a day is a real month. More time, more taken in. That's the whole equation and it's honest.

But here's the part that makes this different from anything you've tried before.

Most training goes stale. You learn something in October, you don't touch it, and by January it's gone — so you learn it again, and that's why so many goalies feel like they're running on the spot.

Our process reaffirms what you've acquired. It doesn't let it go stale. That is the key.

Reinforcement is heaviest at the beginning — deliberately — and it eases as the system recognises your growth and your consistency, judged on your answers and on how long you take to complete things. The platform is watching, and we tell our students that plainly: this all matters.

It applies polite mental pressure. That's on purpose. A goalie who never feels any pressure in training has no practice at handling it — and adversity is the job.

question: What happens in a typical week?
answer:
There isn't a schedule you have to keep up with, and that's deliberate - your hockey week already owns your time.

What a week looks like when it's working: some knowledge work, in pieces small enough to actually do. A chart after your game, and after a practice if you played one. A directive to take onto the ice with you. And a look at what the charts are showing, which is where you find out what to work on next.

Fifteen minutes a day is a real week. More time, more taken in.

The one thing I'd ask is consistency over volume. A goalie who does a little every week beats one who does a lot in bursts, every time.

question: Can my goalie coach use this alongside what we already do?
answer:
Yes, and he loses nothing by it.

A goalie coach with his own methods gets a student who arrives more aware, better prepared and easier to teach. He knows what he's working on, he can describe what he saw, and he has a record of it.

We are not trying to replace anybody. Smarter Goalie is the team behind the team.

And I'd say this to any goalie coach directly: if what you teach and what we teach differ somewhere, that's a conversation worth having, not a problem. I welcome the dialogue. I have never believed there's only one way to do this.

question: Can a whole team, club or organization use it?
answer:
Yes — and it's built to be automated so a club isn't dependent on one person's availability.

The full picture on content, pricing and the degree of support for organizations and other sectors is being defined now, and it will be specific rather than vague when it lands.

What I can tell you is the shape of it. We can support an organization's own camps and clinics with affiliate support — or, in the future, with our own travel teams. The reason that's worth a club's attention is simple: these programs save your goalie families money and put some money back into the organization's coffers.

Most clubs treat goalie development as a cost they can't afford. This is structured so it doesn't have to be.

question: What happens if I take a season off, or stop?
answer:
Nothing is lost. That's the whole point of this.

You can switch the subscription off - take the summer, take longer - pay nothing while it's off, and switch back on for pre-season. Your record is exactly where you left it.

And if you stop altogether and come back in two years, it's still there. Your charts, your answers, what you'd figured out, what you were working on the week you stopped.

Your body will have changed. Your game will have changed. But the understanding doesn't grow out of its clothes, and the markers are where they always were.

You're not ever starting over. That's not a slogan - it's the reason the record exists.

question: Can my parent see everything I write in here?
answer:
Straight answer, because you deserve one.

Your parent holds the account, and if you're under age that's how it has to be. They can see your record - what you're working on, your charts, your ratings, your progress, your time on the site.

What they don't see by default is what you write privately about yourself. That's on purpose. Some of what a goalie puts in here is more honest than what he'd say out loud, and that honesty is what makes the charting worth anything at all. If you were writing for an audience it would stop being a mirror.

How your family handles what they can see is between you and them.

And be honest in here anyway. Nobody is grading you. The chart only works if what goes in is true.

question: How do I deal with the pressure?
answer:
Start here: pressure is a given. Panic is a choice.

Prepare, mentally and physically. Know the opposition, know your own game, arrive rested. Half of what people call pressure is just being under-prepared and knowing it.

Stay in the present. Not the last goal, not the next period. Now.

Use what actually works and has for a long time - breathing, slow and deliberate. Visualisation, rehearsing the saves before you make them. Positive self-talk, reminding yourself what you can already do. A routine you trust.

Focus on the process, not the outcome. The score is not yours to control. The next read is.

And embrace it. Pressure is part of the position and it can work for you. A goalie who never meets pressure in training has no practice at meeting it in a game - which is exactly why our system applies a little of it on purpose.

If it ever becomes too much, talk to someone. Your coach, or a professional. That is strength, not weakness.

question: How do I build confidence that actually lasts?
answer:
Confidence built on results is rented. It leaves the night you lose.

Confidence built on evidence is yours.

That's why we chart. When you can see what you've actually fixed - the thing you couldn't do in October and own by February - that is not a feeling, it's a record. Nobody can take it off you with one bad night.

The rest is habits. Set goals you can actually measure. Reflect after every game honestly. Talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a teammate. Keep learning, because a goalie who understands why something works is harder to shake than one who's just hoping.

You're not ever starting over. Your own history is the proof, and it's right there.

question: What should my pre-game routine be?
answer:
Yours. That's the honest answer - but here's what goes in it.

A warm-up that sharpens the reflexes, not just loosens the body. Specific drills that get you into the rhythm of the game.

Mental preparation. Visualisation, quiet, affirmations - whatever puts you in the right state. Some goalies want silence. Some want music. Both are correct.

How you deal with your teammates. Some talk to their defence, some keep to themselves. Also both correct.

And superstitions, if you have them - the tape, the socks, the meal. I'm not going to talk anyone out of those. If a ritual settles you, it's doing a job.

One warning. Over-preparing is real and it costs you: mental and physical exhaustion, overthinking, second-guessing, and a goalie too rigid to react to what actually happens. Prepared, then let go.

question: How do I balance school with hockey?
answer:
By accepting that you need a life outside this, and that having one makes you better at it, not worse.

The goalies who last have three things. A support system - family, friends, people who are there when it's going badly. Care for the body and the mind, because how you live shows up in how you play. And a life beyond hockey: other interests, other people, something that isn't the rink.

That's not a distraction from the position. It's what stops you burning out in it.

School is the same discipline you're building here - commitment, preparation, doing the work when nobody's watching. You're not splitting yourself between two things. You're practising the same thing twice.

question: What should I eat, and how much sleep do I need?
answer:
These are foundation. Not to hockey — to a balanced life and an athletic life, and hockey sits on top of both.

How you treat your body — your temple — will be directly reflected in how you perform. If not today, then one day soon. And when it shows up it is crippling to performance, which is a hard word and the right one.

That's the part young athletes don't believe until it's already happening. The bill for a badly-run week is not paid that week. It's paid in the third period of a game that mattered, months later, and almost nobody traces it back.

So we chart it — nutrition, hydration, sleep and rest, alongside mental preparation, physical training, game-day routine and how you recover afterwards. Not to lecture anybody. Because seeing your own record show you the connection between how you lived and how you played is worth more than being told it a hundred times.

You are building an athlete first. The goalie is what the athlete does.

question: I face forty shots a night on a struggling team. How do I survive that?
answer:
First - that's a hard place to be and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. The team leans on you, and the pressure is real.

Go back to the basics, and I mean that literally. Positioning, angles, rebound control. When the volume is high, sound fundamentals are worth more than anything flashy, and they're what make you hard to score on with limited help.

Talk. Direct your defence, call out who's dangerous, tell them how you want the puck played. A goalie who organises the front of his net changes what arrives at it.

Set goals you can actually reach. Not "we win." A number of saves. A cap on what you'll allow. Something you control, so the scoreboard doesn't decide how you feel about yourself.

Stay mentally strong and give credit where it's due when things go well. You are one player. You cannot win it alone and you were never supposed to.

And here's the part nobody says: forty shots a night is a development opportunity most goalies never get. You're seeing more real situations in a month than a goalie on a strong team sees in a season.

question: I'm on a strong team and barely see shots. Is that hurting me?
answer:
It might be, and it's worth knowing why so you can do something about it.

A dominant team means fewer game situations - fewer power plays against, fewer penalty kills, fewer high-pressure moments. Those situations are how a goalie develops, and you're not getting them.

It can also mean less meaningful ice time, which is frustrating when you're keen to improve.

There's a quieter risk too: comfort. When games are never close, it's easy to stop being challenged and stop progressing without noticing.

And you don't build mental toughness in games that were never in doubt. You build it in the tight ones, and if you're not getting them you have to find that pressure somewhere else.

So make your practices the game. Bring a directive every time, chart what you're working on, and use Opportunity Time properly. If the games won't challenge you, you challenge yourself.

question: My goalie partner and I don't get along. What do I do?
answer:
Handle it professionally, whichever side of it you're on.

If your partner is getting the big starts: talk to your coach honestly, ask what you need to do, and then keep working. Stay positive and focus on what you control. Learn from your partner - watch what he does well and take it. Be a good teammate to him even when it's hard, because that's noticed. And ask for feedback rather than waiting for it.

If you're the starter: support him, communicate, share what you know, respect his role. Lead by example. Help him be ready for his starts - a good backup makes you better, and a resentful one makes the whole season worse.

If it's genuinely weighing on you, talk to someone about it. A coach, a parent, a professional. That's not weakness.

You are two goalies on one team. The tandem that works out beats the tandem that doesn't, every time.

question: I'm new on the team. How do I earn respect as the goalie?
answer:
You earn it before you make a single save.

Be prepared. On time, in full gear, everything you need. That alone puts you ahead of most.

Be dependable and consistent. Not brilliant once - steady. Steady is what a team learns to trust.

Communicate. Ask questions, share what you see, talk to your defence. A goalie who talks is a goalie who's part of the team.

Be coachable. Take feedback without defending yourself. Listen more than you speak at the start.

Show your work ethic. Not your highlight saves - your effort in the drills nobody enjoys.

And be positive. Teams notice attitude faster than they notice technique.

Respect follows behaviour. It always has.

question: I'm not enjoying it right now. Is that normal?
answer:
Yes. And thank you for saying it, because most goalies don't.

This position asks more of you than any other on the ice, and there are stretches where it takes more than it gives. That is not a sign you've chosen wrong.

Two things worth checking. Are you carrying it alone? Goalies do, and it's the fastest way to stop enjoying anything. Family, friends, a coach - a support system is not a luxury in this position.

And is there anything in your life that isn't hockey right now? The goalies who last have something else. If the rink is the only thing, every bad night is a bad life.

If it's heavier than a rough patch - if it's been there a while and it isn't lifting - talk to someone properly. A parent, your coach, a professional. That's the same good judgement you'd use on an injury you couldn't skate off.

You don't have to decide anything today.

question: My coach pulled me mid-game. How do I come back from that?
answer:
It's a rotten feeling and everyone who has played this position has had it.

On the bench, right then: you're still on the team. How you sit there is seen by everyone, and it says more about you than the goals did.

Afterwards, reflect properly rather than replaying it. What actually happened? Was it your positioning, your reads, your preparation - or was it a night where the game got away from everybody? Watch it if you can. The video never lies, and it's usually kinder than your memory.

Then ask your coach, straight: what did you see, and what do you want from me next time? That question changes how a coach sees you.

And then let it go. Reflect, learn, recover, move on. Dwelling on it costs you the next game as well as the last one.

One bad night is data. It is not a verdict.

question: What is a "development support system", and how is it different from lessons?
answer:
A lesson ends. This does not.

That is the whole difference and it sounds smaller than it is. A lesson gives you an hour and a correction. What happens to that correction on the Tuesday three weeks later, when nobody is watching and you have forgotten which part mattered? Usually nothing. That is why so many goalies feel like they are running on the spot after years of lessons.

A support system is there between the lessons. It holds your record, it tells you what to work on next, and it reaffirms what you have already acquired rather than letting it go stale.

We are not replacing your coach. We are the team behind the team.

question: You say it meets me where I am. How do you know where I am?
answer:
Because you tell us, and then you keep telling us.

It starts with a Baseline Profile - what you have played, what you have been taught, what you can already do, what you know you cannot. Then it never stops, because your own charting keeps the picture current.

That is the part most systems get wrong. They assess you once and then coach the goalie you were in September.

Where you are is not a fixed thing. It is a moving one, and the system moves with it.

question: What does "nothing left to the imagination" mean in practice?
answer:
It means you are never told to figure it out.

Most goalies are handed advice and left to work out the rest. "Be square." "Cut down the angle." "Be more aggressive." Every one of those is a conclusion with the working removed, and a goalie who acts on it is guessing with good intentions.

Nothing left to the imagination means the why comes with the what. Where you stand, why there, what changes it, and how you know you got it right.

You should never have to invent the part your coach did not say.

question: What are the pillars, and do I have to do all of them?
answer:
They are the whole of the position, broken into parts that can actually be worked on. MindSet. Skating Tech. The 7 Angle-Marker System. The 6 Zone - 7 Point System. Form Tech. The Game Performance Charting System. The Practice System. Lifestyle & Hockey.

You do not have to do all of them, and you do not have to do them in order. Plenty of goalies come in with one thing that is costing them and start there.

But understand what they are. They are not eight subjects. They are eight angles on one goalie, and they lean on each other - your skating decides your angles, your angles decide your form, your mind decides whether any of it holds up in the third period.

Start where it hurts. You will end up in the others.

question: What is the 7 Angle-Marker System?
answer:
Seven markers that tell you exactly where you are above the icing line.

Not roughly. Exactly. It is the goalie's GPS, and it answers the question that "be square" never does: square to what, from where, at what depth.

A goalie who owns it can tell you precisely where he was on a goal against - not just that he was wrong. That is a completely different conversation to have with yourself.

I created it in 1977 because nobody had written it down.

question: What is the 6 Zone - 7 Point System(TM), and why is it a separate system?
answer:
Because it is a different problem, and treating it as an extension of your angles is exactly why so many goals go in from behind the net.

Above the icing line you are managing a shooter. Below it you are defending your own house against a player whose first job is to take your advantage away, and who is working on the fact that most goalies have only ever been taught to follow one thing at a time.

The 7 Angle-Marker System handles the first. The 6 Zone - 7 Point System(TM) handles the second: seven grid lines numbered one through seven, points three, four and five behind the net, six zones built on the grid. The grid defines the zones. The zones define the challenge, and the challenge decides how that player gets played.

It is positional strategy and tactical play, and its whole purpose is that the advantage stays yours.

Most goalies have been taught half a rink and have never been told that is what happened to them.

question: You say video never lies. What am I supposed to see in it that I cannot see now?
answer:
The difference between the game you remember and the game you played.

That gap is real, it is bigger than any goalie expects, and it is the single most useful thing video gives you. Memory does not just fade - it edits, and it edits in the same direction every time.

You will see that you were set later than you thought. That you were further out, or further back. That the goal you have been sick about was going in against anybody, and that the routine one you forgot about was the actual problem.

The video never lies. Your memory does it kindly, which is worse.

question: What does "raising your evaluation ability" actually mean?
answer:
Getting better at seeing your own game accurately.

It is a skill, it is trainable, and almost nobody trains it. Most goalies evaluate themselves with two settings: I played well, or I was terrible. Both are usually about the scoreboard rather than the performance.

Raising it means you can look at a period and say what actually happened, in specifics, without flattering yourself or punishing yourself.

That is where the 5-Star Engine goes - Learning, Self-Evaluation, Self-Awareness, Self-Adjusting, Self-Coaching. Every star above the first one depends on being able to see straight.

question: You say gaps are not failures. So what is a gap?
answer:
The distance between where you are and where you are going. Nothing more sinister than that.

Every goalie has them, at every level. A gap is not something wrong with you - it is the next thing, identified, so you can go and do something about it instead of hoping.

Failure is not part of this system. A goal against is information. A rating that dips is information. Nothing is being subtracted from you.

A gap is not a verdict. It is the roadmap.

question: What is a Baseline Profile, and how do I get one?
answer:
It is the honest picture of where you are the day you walk in.

What you have played and for how long. What you have been taught and by whom. What you can do, what you cannot, what you have never been shown. What other sports you have played, which matters more than you would think.

You get it by answering, properly and honestly. It is not a test and there is no score to be afraid of - a baseline that flatters you produces a plan for a goalie who does not exist.

And it is not a one-time thing. It is the floor your record is built on, and it grows with you.

question: What is the "intuitive system"?
answer:
The point at which the knowing stops being conscious.

Everything we teach starts deliberate. You think about where you are. You check your depth. You work out what he is going to do. That is normal and it is slow.

Then, with enough correct repetition, it moves. You stop calculating your position and start feeling it. You stop deciding to read and just read.

That is what the Feel Factor is - the same work run so many times it no longer needs looking. Feeling is the goal. The glance is the enemy.

The system is intuitive at the end. It is not intuitive at the start, and any coach who tells you it is has skipped the part that takes the work.

question: You say most goalies have a puzzle with no border. What are the borders?
answer:
The things that hold everything else in place.

Most goalies have pieces. A drill they were shown. A tip from a coach. Something they copied off a goalie they watched. Real pieces, some of them good - and no edges, so nothing connects and nothing tells them where a new piece goes.

The borders are the systems. Where you are, above the line and below it. How you move. How you set. How you read. How you record it and how you fix it.

Once the border is down, every piece you pick up afterwards has somewhere to go. That is why goalies in this system say new information sticks now when it never used to.

question: What does "the goalie decides when, why, where and how" look like on the ice?
answer:
It looks like a goalie who is never surprised.

Watch two goalies on the same play. One is responding to what has already happened to him - the puck moves, he moves, always second. The other has already decided what he is going to do if it goes there, and if it goes there instead.

That is the difference between reacting and deciding, and it is most of what separates a technically fine goalie from one who is genuinely hard to score on.

An Intelligent Athletic Goaltender knows the options, anticipates the play, and dictates the terms. Everybody else is answering.

question: What is the Mind-Vault?
answer:
Where the valuable things are kept.

It has three jobs. It stores and retrieves - the reads, the corrections, the things you have already solved, so you do not solve them twice. It filters the noise, because a goalie hears a great deal in a season and most of it is not useful. And it masters the reset, which is how you get from one moment to the next without carrying the last one.

It is the discipline of building a place where only the most valuable foundational thoughts and behaviours are kept. For game performance, and for life in general.

If you cannot control what is inside, you cannot control what is outside.

question: "Logic, math, science - every read." How does that work in a game?
answer:
You are not doing equations. Your brain is, and it is doing them whether you help it or not.

Where is the puck going. How fast. Where will it be when I get there. Where can he actually put it from where he is standing. That is computation, it is running constantly, and you are not conscious of any of it.

I call it Mental Math. You already own more of it than you know - every time you have caught something, fielded something, judged a ball in the air, you were running it.

What we do is give it better information to work with. Position, angles, markers. The math does not change. What changes is how good the numbers going into it are.

question: Performance versus outcome - which one am I judged on here?
answer:
Performance. Always.

Outcome is the scoreboard. Performance is what you actually did. They are related and they are not the same, and a goalie who cannot separate them is at the mercy of luck.

You can be excellent in a loss and fortunate in a win. Judge yourself by the result and you will be wrong about half the time - and worse, you will not know which half.

You control one of those two. We measure that one.

question: Why does the site say my most important relationship is with the net?
answer:
Because it is the only thing on the ice that never moves.

Players move. The puck moves. The play changes every second. The net is behind you, it is always in the same place, and everything you do is measured against it - your angle, your depth, whether you are square, whether you have created coverage or just stood in the way.

Most goalies have a relationship with the puck and only a rough idea of the net. They glance for the post. They reach for it. And in that half-second the play has moved on.

Build the relationship with the net, the crease and the white ice beyond it and you stop checking. You start knowing.

question: What is Game IQ, and how do you assess it?
answer:
Game IQ is what you understand about the situation you are standing in.

Not how athletic you are. Not how quick. What you know - about the shooter, the angle, the time on the clock, what your defence is doing, what he can and cannot do from where he is.

We assess it the way we assess everything else: against what actually happened. Your read, your reasoning, your chart, and then the video. The gap between what you thought was happening and what was happening is measurable, and closing it is the work.

It is the most improvable thing in the position and the least trained.

question: What does "know what you do not know" mean?
answer:
That the dangerous gaps are the ones you cannot see.

A goalie who knows he is poor at something will work on it. A goalie who does not know is the one who repeats it for three seasons and cannot understand why he is stuck.

Ask a goalie if he goes down before the shot and most cannot tell you. That is not a failing - nobody has ever shown them how to notice it.

So the first job is not fixing. It is seeing. That is why the charting, the video and the honest baseline come before anything else.

You cannot fix what you have not found.

question: What does "coach yourself between sessions" actually involve?
answer:
Arriving with a job, and knowing whether you did it.

Concretely: you chart after your game. The chart shows a gap. That becomes one directive - one thing, not five, because you cannot build feel on five things at once. You take that directive onto the ice, including into the dead minutes of a team practice. Then you chart again and see whether it moved.

Chart, directive, practice, chart. That is the Development Loop and it is the engine of the whole thing.

It is not a replacement for coaching. It is what makes coaching worth more when you get it.

question: What is a Factor Ratio?
answer:
A charting measure. It is how we put a number on something that usually gets described with an adjective.

Coaches say a goalie is "pretty good" at something. That is not information you can work with, and it certainly does not tell you whether it improved.

A Factor Ratio does. It gives you a figure you can watch over time, so development becomes something you can see rather than something you feel.

It is a measure, not a place on the ice. Worth saying, because people assume anything with a number attached must be a zone.

question: What is the Technical Eye?
answer:
The gap between what you think happened and what did.

Every goalie has one and most have never measured it. You come off the ice certain you were square, certain you were set, certain that one was unstoppable. Then you watch it.

Closing that gap is most of the development in this system, and it is why we ask you to chart before you look at the video. Your version first. Then the truth. The distance between them is the number that matters.

A goalie with a sharp Technical Eye can coach himself. One without it is guessing about his own game.

question: What is the Feel Factor?
answer:
Knowing exactly where you are in your net without looking for it.

Most goalies check. They glance at the post, they reach for it - and in that half-second the play has moved. When your markers are trained, you stop checking and you start knowing.

That is the Feel Factor, and it is built, not born. It is the thing goalies tell us changed their game fastest, because it hands back the half-second everyone else spends looking.

Feeling is the goal. The glance is the enemy.

question: What is a good goal and a weak goal, and who decides which it was?
answer:
You do. First, and honestly.

A good goal is one that was going in against anybody - a shot that beat you because it was better than any goalie standing there. A weak goal is one where something on your side gave it up. Position, read, preparation, recovery.

Deciding which is which is a skill, not an opinion, and it is one of the most valuable things you will learn here. Get it wrong in one direction and you punish yourself for things you could not control. Get it wrong in the other and you never fix the thing that keeps costing you.

You chart it. Then the video settles it. Then, if you are working with me, we look at it together.

Nobody is grading you. You are learning to grade yourself accurately, which is a harder and far more useful skill.

[COACH TO RULE - the site uses "weak goal" as a charting term. "Weak" is banned as a rating word in our own system. Confirm the term or give the replacement and it changes everywhere.]

question: What is Designated Training, and who sets my one directive?
answer:
Designated Training is targeted work, chosen because your own record said so. Not whatever the session happens to contain. One specific thing, worked deliberately.

Ordinary practice is exposure - you do a lot and hope some of it lands. Designated Training is treatment. You know what you are fixing and you know why.

Who sets the directive depends on where you are. At the start it comes from your charting and from me. As you climb - Self-Evaluation, Self-Awareness, Self-Adjusting - more of it comes from you.

At five stars you set it yourself. That is what Self-Coaching means, and it does not mean you no longer need a coach. It means you know what support you need and you can ask for it precisely.

question: What are strong side and weak side, and how do you close the gap?
answer:
Every goalie has a better side. Almost none of them know by how much.

It shows up in your movement, your recovery, your reach, your comfort - and shooters find it long before you admit it. A side you avoid is a side you will keep being beaten on.

We do not fix it by hammering the poor side until it hurts. We find out first: what is the actual difference, is it edges, is it flexibility, is it a habit, is it something you started doing after an injury three years ago.

Then it gets one directive at a time.

Closing that gap is one of the fastest visible changes in a goalie's game, because you are not learning something new. You are collecting something you already half own.

question: My rating dips. What happens next?
answer:
Nothing punishing. The system does not scold you.

A dip is information, and its job is to point at something. So what happens is that the material which lifts that specific gap opens up - drawn from what you have already been taught, aimed at the thing that actually moved.

That is the loop the whole platform runs on: the chart shows the gap, the gap becomes one directive, the directive goes onto the ice, and you chart again.

A gap is not a failure. It is the roadmap.

question: You say this is a system, not a program. What is the difference to me?
answer:
A program is a set of things to do. A system is a way of understanding.

It matters most when something changes. A goalie taught a program has a routine, and when his body changes or his level changes or a coach asks for something different, the routine stops fitting and he has to be given a new one.

A goalie taught a system carries it. The markers did not move. The reads did not change. What he understands still applies to a body he has not met before.

That is why goalies who grow six inches lose a program and keep a system.

question: What happens to my record if I stop?
answer:
Nothing is lost. That is the whole point of this.

Switch the subscription off - take the summer, take longer - and your record is exactly where you left it. Come back in two years and it is still there. Your charts, your answers, what you had figured out, what you were working on the week you stopped.

Your body will have changed. Your game will have changed. But the understanding does not grow out of its clothes, and the markers are where they always were.

You are not ever starting over. That is not a slogan - it is the reason the record exists.

question: Why is MindSet the first pillar when I came here to stop pucks?
answer:
Because if you cannot control what's inside, you cannot control what's outside.

That is not a motivational line. It is a sequence. Every save starts as something you see, becomes something you read, and only then becomes something you do. The reading happens inside, before anything physical happens at all.

One thing to be clear about, because it gets misunderstood: this is not a gate. Plenty of very good goalies have the mental game as their softest pillar. Being first does not mean you must master it before anything else is allowed to happen.

It is first because it is where control begins.

question: My goalie falls apart after one bad goal. What is actually happening?
answer:
He is still in the goal that already went in, and the game has moved on without him.

That is not weakness and it is not a personality flaw. It is a goalie with nowhere to put it. Every goalie gets scored on. The ones who look unshakeable are not feeling less - they have somewhere to set it down and a way to get back to the next read.

That place can be built. It is one of the specific things we work on, and it is a skill rather than a temperament.

The short version for you as a parent: he does not need to care less. He needs somewhere to keep it.

question: What is the difference between performance and outcome, and why does it matter?
answer:
Outcome is the scoreboard. Performance is what you actually did.

They are related and they are not the same, and a goalie who cannot separate them is at the mercy of luck. You can be excellent in a loss and fortunate in a win. Judge yourself by the outcome and you will be wrong about half the time - and worse, you will not know which half.

You control one of those two. Only one.

Learning to see the difference is where honest self-evaluation starts, and it is the reason we measure what we measure.

question: How do I handle pressure instead of hoping it does not turn up?
answer:
Start by accepting the first half of the sentence. Pressure is a given. Panic is a choice.

Hoping it stays away is a plan that fails on the night it matters, because that is exactly the night it arrives.

What works is preparation you trust, a routine you own, and having met pressure before in a place where it did not cost you anything. That last one is why our system deliberately keeps a small, honest weight on you rather than making everything frictionless. A goalie who never meets pressure in training has no practice at meeting it in a game.

Adversity is the job. We would rather you had rehearsed it.

question: How is goalie skating different from player skating?
answer:
A player skates to get somewhere. A goalie skates to arrive in a position to make a save - balanced, square, and able to move again immediately.

A player can finish a stride off balance and lose nothing. A goalie who arrives off balance has already lost the save, and he lost it before the shot was taken.

That is why team skating time only partly serves you. It is good work. It is not your work.

question: Why am I gassed by the third period when I barely left my crease?
answer:
Because distance is not what tires a goalie. Waste is.

Two movements where one would have done. Drifting, then correcting. Being late and having to hurry. None of that shows up as distance travelled and all of it shows up in the third period.

Fitness matters and we chart it. But a fit goalie who moves badly still runs out - he just runs out slightly later.

The question worth asking is not how hard you worked. It is how much of it you needed to.

question: What is Movement, Energy and Time?
answer:
No wasted movement. No wasted energy. No wasted time.

And they are one thing, not three. Waste one and you waste all three - an unnecessary movement costs energy, and the energy costs you time you needed later in the shift.

It is the efficiency principle underneath everything we teach. When you watch a goalie who looks calm and always seems to be there already, you are not watching fast feet. You are watching someone who stopped spending what he did not need to spend.

question: My goalie is always half a second late. Is that just slow feet?
answer:
Rarely.

Late usually means the read started late, not that the body moved late. And a goalie who is in the wrong place has further to travel - half a second late is very often two feet out of position.

Both of those are fixable. Feet are the hardest thing on that list to change and they are almost never the actual cause.

Before you conclude anything about his quickness, there is one honest question worth answering: is he set before the release? Most goalies who look slow are not.

question: Why does stopping matter more than starting?
answer:
Because anyone can go.

Getting moving is the easy half. Arriving under control - balanced, square, ready to move again - is the half that decides whether the movement was worth making.

A goalie who can start but not stop spends the whole game overshooting and correcting, which is another way of describing wasted movement, wasted energy and wasted time.

Control at the end of the movement is the skill. The push is just the price of admission.

question: "You were off your angle." What does that actually mean?
answer:
It means something was wrong, and it does not tell you what - which is why hearing it rarely helps.

Being on your angle has two parts. The front of your body centred to the puck, and your back centred to the net. Miss either one and you can look square while being beaten.

Skating backwards especially, a goalie drifts off the line between the puck and the net and opens a side without ever feeling it happen. It feels square the whole way. It is not.

So the useful question back to your coach is: which part was missing? And the reason our system exists is to turn that vague sentence into a specific, findable place on the ice.

question: How do I know where I am in my net without looking for the post?
answer:
By building a relationship with the ice you play on - the net, the crease, the white ice beyond it - until your position is something you feel rather than something you check.

Most goalies check. They glance, they reach for the post, and in that half-second the play has moved.

We call it the Feel Factor, and it is built rather than born. It is the single thing goalies tell us changed their game fastest, because it hands back the half-second everyone else spends looking.

Feeling is the goal. The glance is the enemy.

question: Why seven markers instead of just telling me to be square?
answer:
Because "be square" is advice, not information.

Square to what, from where, at what depth? A goalie told to be square and left to work out the rest is guessing with good intentions, and guessing is what we are trying to remove.

Seven markers give a goalie something no instruction can: positional certainty. He knows where he is, and therefore where he needs to be next, without checking.

I created it in 1977 because nobody had written it down. It is the goalie's GPS, and it is the reason a Smarter Goalie can tell you exactly where he was on a goal against - not just that he was wrong.

question: What is the difference between being centred and being positionally strong?
answer:
Centred is one thing being right. Positionally strong is everything being right at once.

You can be perfectly centred to the puck and still be beaten - wrong depth, wrong relationship to the net behind you, arriving unbalanced, or square to a puck while the player carrying it has options you have not accounted for.

Centred is a snapshot. Positionally strong is a state you can hold while everything moves.

That distinction is most of what separates a goalie who is technically fine from one who is genuinely hard to score on.

question: Why is there a second system? I thought the angles were the system.
answer:
Because behind your net the advantage is up for grabs, and almost nobody has been taught how to keep it.

Above the icing line you are managing a shooter. He is in front of you and the question is angles.

Below it, someone has walked into your house. He is not trying to score from back there - he is trying to take something off you first. Your position, your balance, your read. He wants you to commit, and then he will use what you gave up.

That is a tactical problem, not an angles problem, and it needs its own system.

The 7 Angle-Marker System governs the play in front of you. The 6 Zone - 7 Point System(TM) governs the play behind you. Two systems, one umbrella, one goalie who runs both.

question: What is the 6 Zone - 7 Point System(TM), in one sentence?
answer:
Positional strategy and tactical play for the goalie's house - the area behind and around your own net - built on a grid of seven lines numbered one through seven, with points three, four and five behind the net, and six zones defined on that grid.

Here is what the grid actually does, and it is worth understanding even if you never join us.

The grid defines the zones. The zones define the challenge - because where that player is, and where the puck is, decide together what he is able to do to you. And the challenge decides how he gets played.

So it is not a map of where to stand. It is a read of what you are facing and what to do about it.

The purpose of the whole thing is one thing: the advantage stays in your house.

question: What do I do when the puck goes behind my net? (Pillar 4)
answer:
You understand how to play both the man and the puck. That understanding is the whole skill.

Most goalies have never been taught it as one thing. They track the puck and have no idea what he is setting up. Or they watch him and get beaten by a puck that went somewhere they were not expecting. Both of those are a goalie reacting to one half of a situation.

And the two are not always in the same place. The puck can be in one spot and his body somewhere else entirely - that is not an accident, that is him working on you.

Understanding both means you know what each of them can do, and what the two of them together make possible from where they are. Once you know that, you are not tracking anything. You already know the short list of what can happen next.

Where he is and where the puck is tell you that. It is what the zones are for.

And once you accept that it is your house, the whole thing gets simpler. He is a visitor. He does not get to decide how it goes in there.

question: How do I know where to be when the play is below the goal line?
answer:
By understanding what he can do from where he is, with the puck where it is, before he does it.

That is the difference between a goalie who is reacting behind his net and one who is running it. The reacting goalie is answering a question that has already been asked. The other one already knew the two or three things that were possible and had decided about all of them.

The grid is what makes that possible. Each zone brings its own challenge - a different set of options for him, a different answer from you.

That is why "somewhere near your post" is not a strategy. It is a guess dressed up as a position, and against a good player it fails often enough to cost you games.

Understanding him and the puck. Not just knowing where you are.

question: How does this fit with the 7 Angle-Marker System - do I run both at once?
answer:
The puck decides which one you are in, and the changeover between them is itself a skill.

They do not overlap and they do not compete. Above the icing line, the markers. Below it, the zones and the points. You are never running both systems at the same moment - you are running the right one, and switching cleanly.

The handover is where goals get scored. That moment when the play comes out from behind the net, or goes back into it, is the two or three seconds a game where most goalies are working from nothing at all. They have left one system and not yet arrived in the other.

Get the handover clean and you have closed the last gap in your own end.

Both systems, under one umbrella. That is a Smarter Goalie.

question: What is the set-crouch, and is there only one?
answer:
There is not one. That is the first thing worth knowing, and it surprises most goalies.

A set-crouch is your ready position - where your body is when the shot is about to happen. But the right one changes with the situation. Higher when the puck is further out or you need to see over traffic. Lower when it is close, or you are sealing the ice. Wider when stability matters more than the push.

We teach a family of them, and we teach you to find your own within it, because a set-crouch built for someone else's body is a borrowed answer.

Yours is the one worth having.

question: What does "maximum coverage, minimal movement" mean?
answer:
That the goal is to take away as much net as possible while spending as little as possible to do it.

Those two pull against each other, which is the whole problem. Big movements cover ground and cost you balance, energy and recovery time. Small movements are cheap and may not get you there.

The answer is not to move less. It is to need to move less - which comes from being in the right place before the play forces you somewhere.

A goalie who looks unhurried usually is not faster. He is just spending less.

question: Why do my rebounds keep coming back to the slot?
answer:
Because a rebound is decided before the puck arrives, not after.

Where it goes is a product of how you were set, what your base was doing, and what your hands and stick were prepared to do with it. A poor base gives up an uncontrolled rebound no matter how good the initial save looked.

Most goalies think of rebound control as something that happens at the moment of contact. It is really three phases, and the one that matters most happens before the shot.

Sending a puck somewhere it cannot hurt you is a decision. It is available to you, and it is trainable.

question: Am I going down too much?
answer:
Possibly - but here is the better question, and most goalies cannot answer it: are you going down before the shot?

If you are dropping on every shot, can you actually detect that you are going down before the release? Most cannot, and that is not a failing. Nobody has ever shown them how to notice it.

Going down is not the problem. Going down early is, because it hands the shooter his decision - he is now choosing from what is left, and what is left is up.

Learning to see it in yourself is the first step, and it is exactly the kind of thing your own record will show you before anyone tells you.

question: What does it mean that goalies create coverage?
answer:
That coverage is something you make, not something you have.

Your size is fixed. What is not fixed is how much net a shooter can actually see and use, and that is determined by where you are and how you are set - not by how big you are.

Two goalies of identical build can present completely different amounts of net from the same shot. One created coverage. The other stood in the way and hoped.

That is why we spend so much time on position before we spend any on athleticism. The athleticism is what saves you when the position was not enough.

question: What is charting, and why does it matter so much here? (Pillar 6)
answer:
Charting is you recording what actually happened, in your own ratings and your own words.

It matters because memory lies, and it lies in the same direction every time. Every goalie remembers the game he thinks he played. The chart remembers the game he played. The gap between those two is where the development is.

It is a mirror, not a test. Nobody is grading you and there is nothing to fail - which is exactly why it only works if you are honest in it.

Then it accumulates. And a record that goes back three seasons is worth something no single lesson can be.

question: What does a chart show that a coach watching from the bench does not?
answer:
Pattern.

A coach sees tonight. A good one sees tonight clearly and remembers a few things from last month. Nobody watching from a bench can hold sixty games in their head and tell you which situation keeps costing you - because it is not one dramatic thing, it is a small thing recurring.

The chart holds all of it, and patterns surface that nobody could have spotted by watching.

It also shows something a coach genuinely cannot see: what you thought was happening. The difference between that and what the video shows is one of the most useful measurements in this entire system.

question: My rating dipped. What happens next? (Pillar 6)
answer:
Nothing punishing. The system does not scold you.

A dip is information, and its job is to point at something. So what happens is that the material which lifts that specific gap opens up - drawn from what you have already been taught, aimed at the thing that actually moved.

That is the loop the whole platform runs on: the chart shows the gap, the gap becomes one directive, the directive goes onto the ice, and you chart again.

A gap is not a failure. It is the roadmap.

question: How much of a team practice is actually any use to a goalie?
answer:
Less than you would hope, and more than most goalies get out of it.

A great deal of a team practice is not built for you. Drills with no goalie involvement. Skating blocks designed for players. Long stretches at the boards while a coach explains something to everyone else.

Most goalies treat that as dead time. It does not have to be.

The difference is whether you arrive with a job. A goalie with a directive can use time that a goalie without one simply loses - and over a season that difference is enormous.

question: What is Designated Training? (Pillar 7)
answer:
Targeted work, chosen because your own record said so.

Not whatever the session happens to contain. Not a general skate. One specific thing, identified from your charting, worked deliberately.

The difference matters. Ordinary practice is exposure - you do a lot and hope some of it lands. Designated Training is treatment. You know what you are fixing and you know why.

It is also what makes the fifteen minutes a goalie actually controls worth more than the ninety he does not.

question: What do I do when the puck is at the other end of the rink?
answer:
You work. And I mean physically, at your net, not standing there thinking about it.

I asked my own coaches for this as a player. When the team went to the boards for an explanation, I went to my net and worked my game. When there was a twenty-minute skating block, I skated part of it and then went and did what I actually needed - because goalie skating is not player skating.

You ask your coach in advance. It is a cooperative arrangement, not going freelance, and most coaches say yes because it costs them nothing.

We call it Opportunity Time. A bored goalie is a goalie who has not been given a job.

question: Why do I need a directive before I step on the ice?
answer:
Because without one you will practise what you are already good at. Everyone does. It feels better.

A directive is one thing, chosen before you arrive, drawn from what your record says needs attention. One - not five. You cannot build feel on five things at once.

It also changes what the whole session is worth. The same ninety minutes with a directive produces something measurable; without one it produces a nice sweat.

Acknowledge it, focus on it, stay with it. That sequence is how something becomes yours.

question: How do I practise on my own without a shooter?
answer:
More than you would think, and some of the most valuable work needs nobody at all.

Positioning, movement, edges, your relationship to the net and the crease, your set-crouch - none of that requires a puck coming at you. Nor does the knowledge work, or the review of your own footage.

A shooter or two makes it faster and we would always take them. But a goalie who believes he cannot develop without a full practice is a goalie who develops twice a week instead of six times.

Plenty of goalies do their most important work away from a roster.

question: What should I eat, and how much sleep do I actually need? (Pillar 8)
answer:
These are foundation - not to hockey, to a balanced life and an athletic life, and hockey sits on top of both.

How you treat your body will be directly reflected in how you perform. If not today, then one day soon.

Here is the part young athletes do not believe until it is happening: the bill for a badly-run week is not paid that week. It is paid in the third period of a game that mattered, months later, and almost nobody traces it back.

So we chart it - alongside everything else. Not to lecture anybody. Because seeing your own record show you the connection is worth more than being told it a hundred times.

question: How do I balance school with hockey? (Pillar 8)
answer:
By having a life that is bigger than the rink, which turns out to make you better at the rink rather than worse.

The goalies who last have three things: people around them, care for the body and the mind, and something in their life that is not hockey. The ones who burn out at fifteen usually had only the third one missing.

And school is not competing with this. It is the same discipline - preparation, commitment, doing the work when nobody is watching. You are practising the same thing twice.

question: Does off-ice training matter for a goalie?
answer:
Yes, and probably more than for anyone else on the ice.

The position asks for flexibility, agility, balance, core strength, and the endurance to stay sharp for sixty minutes without a shift change. None of that is built on the ice.

Stretching alone does more than most goalies realise - range of motion, injury prevention, balance, recovery, and reaction time.

We are not going to hand you somebody else's programme. What matters first is understanding that the athlete underneath the goalie is the thing being built. The goalie is what the athlete does.

question: My goalie had a growth spurt and lost his game. What happened?
answer:
His frame changed and his game has not caught up to it yet.

New height, new weight, new balance point, new reach, and gear that now sits differently. Everything he owned still works - it is just being executed by a body he has not met before.

This is one of the most misread things in youth goaltending. Coaches see regression. Parents worry. What is actually happening is re-calibration.

And here is the difference with a goalie who has been taught a system rather than a style: a style belonged to the old body and has to be rebuilt. A system carries across. The markers did not move. The understanding did not grow out of its clothes.

He is not starting over. He is adapting - and the growth is not a setback. It is the beginning of a new era.

question: What is the Maintenance Program?
answer:
The part almost nobody talks about, because it is not as exciting as getting better.

What you do not maintain, you lose. Quietly, without noticing, until a game shows you - and then you learn it all again, which is why so many goalies feel like they are running on the spot after years of work.

So there are two journeys happening at once inside every goalie. Development, which everybody sees. And maintenance, which keeps what you have already built from slipping away.

We built four pillars to hold the second one. Together they are what stops your best season being something you look back on.
